tips.title: An equation is a recipe in moles
tips.body: Read $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2}$ as *one mole of magnesium reacts with **two** moles of hydrochloric acid*. The big numbers are the ratio, and every reacting-mass calculation is that ratio applied to the amounts you were given.

tips.title: Mass, moles, ratio, moles, mass
tips.body: Every reacting-mass question is the same five moves: **mass → moles** (divide by Mr) → **apply the equation ratio** → **moles → mass** (multiply by Mr). Write those five boxes out and fill them in; the calculation cannot then go astray.

tips.title: The limiting reactant is not the smaller mass
tips.body: Divide each reactant's moles by **its own big number in the equation**. The smallest answer is the one that runs out first. Comparing raw masses, or even raw moles, gets this wrong whenever the ratio is not 1 : 1.

tips.title: The excess reactant is left over
tips.body: Whatever is not limiting is **in excess**, and some of it is still there at the end. Questions often ask how much is left: work out how much actually reacted using the ratio, then subtract from what you started with.

tips.title: Balancing from masses runs backwards
tips.body: Given the masses of everything, turn each into **moles**, then divide them all by the **smallest** to get a simple whole-number ratio. Those numbers are the balancing numbers. It is the ordinary calculation run in reverse.

steps.title: Reading an equation in moles
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

A balanced equation does more than show that atoms are conserved. It gives the **ratio in which substances react**, and that ratio is in **moles**.

$$\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2}$$

reads as: **one** mole of magnesium reacts with **two** moles of hydrochloric acid to give **one** mole of magnesium chloride and **one** mole of hydrogen.

The ratio is **not** a ratio of masses. One mole of magnesium is $24\text{ g}$ and two moles of $\mathrm{HCl}$ are $73\text{ g}$ — nothing like each other. The **moles** are in the simple ratio; the masses are whatever those moles happen to weigh.

**Masses still balance overall.** For $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$:

- left: $2 \times 24 = 48\text{ g}$ of magnesium, plus $32\text{ g}$ of oxygen
- right: $2 \times 40 = 80\text{ g}$ of magnesium oxide
- and $48 + 32 = 80$ ✓

That check is worth doing on every answer: if the masses on each side do not agree, something has gone wrong.

check.solution: The **2** in front of HCl is the number of moles that react with one mole of magnesium.

steps.title: Calculating a reacting mass
steps.body: Five moves, always in the same order. Write the equation, convert the mass you were given into moles, use the equation ratio, convert back to mass.

visuals.problem: What mass of carbon dioxide is produced when 50 g of calcium carbonate decomposes completely? (Mr: CaCO3 = 100, CO2 = 44)

steps.note: the ratio of carbonate to carbon dioxide is 1 : 1
this is the step the equation provides

visuals.problem: What mass of magnesium oxide is made from 48 g of magnesium? (Mr: Mg = 24, MgO = 40)

steps.note: the ratio of magnesium to oxide is 2 : 2, that is 1 : 1
equal numbers, because the big numbers match

check.prompt: What mass of carbon dioxide, in grams, is produced when 25 g of calcium carbonate decomposes completely? (Mr: CaCO₃ = 100, CO₂ = 44)
check.solution: Moles $= \dfrac{25}{100} = 0.25$; the ratio is $1:1$, so mass $= 0.25 \times 44 = $ **11 g**.

steps.title: Limiting reactants
steps.body:
When two reactants are mixed, they are rarely present in exactly the ratio the equation demands. One runs out first and **stops the reaction**: that one is the **limiting reactant**, because it limits how much product can form. The other is **in excess**, and some of it is left over at the end.

Industry deliberately uses an **excess** of the cheaper reactant, so that all of the expensive one is used up.

**Finding the limiting reactant** takes one extra step that students routinely skip:

1. Convert each reactant to **moles**.
2. **Divide each by its own big number** in the equation.
3. The **smallest** answer is the limiting reactant.

Step 2 is the one that matters. For $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$ with $0.3\text{ mol}$ of magnesium and $0.1\text{ mol}$ of oxygen:

- magnesium: $0.3 \div 2 = 0.15$
- oxygen: $0.1 \div 1 = 0.1$ ← smaller, so **oxygen is limiting**

Magnesium is in excess even though there is *more* of it, because the equation demands twice as much of it.

**The product comes from the limiting reactant.** Oxygen is limiting at $0.1\text{ mol}$, and the ratio $\mathrm{O_2} : \mathrm{MgO}$ is $1 : 2$, so $0.2\text{ mol}$ of magnesium oxide forms — a mass of $0.2 \times 40 = 8\text{ g}$.

**How much excess is left?** The $0.1\text{ mol}$ of oxygen consumed $0.2\text{ mol}$ of magnesium, so $0.3 - 0.2 = 0.1\text{ mol}$ of magnesium remains.

props.title: Divide by the big number before comparing — this is the step most often missed

boxes.title: Excess reactant

check.prompt: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, a mixture contains 0.4 mol of hydrogen and 0.3 mol of oxygen. Which is limiting?
options: Hydrogen, because 0.4 ÷ 2 = 0.2 is smaller than 0.3 ÷ 1
Oxygen, because there is less of it
Hydrogen, because there is more of it
Neither, because they are in the correct ratio
check.solution: Divide each by its balancing number: hydrogen gives $0.4 \div 2 = 0.2$, oxygen gives $0.3 \div 1 = 0.3$. The smaller is hydrogen, so **hydrogen is limiting** — even though there are more moles of it.

steps.title: Using moles to balance an equation
steps.body:
The calculation also runs **backwards**. Given the masses of everything that reacted, you can work out the **balancing numbers**.

1. Convert every mass to **moles**.
2. Divide all the moles by the **smallest** of them.
3. Round to the nearest **simple whole numbers** — those are the balancing numbers.

**Worked through.** $4.8\text{ g}$ of magnesium reacts with $3.2\text{ g}$ of oxygen to give $8.0\text{ g}$ of magnesium oxide.

- Mg: $\dfrac{4.8}{24} = 0.2\text{ mol}$
- $\mathrm{O_2}$: $\dfrac{3.2}{32} = 0.1\text{ mol}$
- MgO: $\dfrac{8.0}{40} = 0.2\text{ mol}$

Divide each by the smallest, $0.1$:

$$2 : 1 : 2$$

so the equation is $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$.

**A check that costs nothing**: $4.8 + 3.2 = 8.0$, so mass is conserved. If your masses do not add up, the data or your arithmetic is wrong before you start.

**Ratios rarely come out exactly.** Experimental masses give something like $1.98 : 1 : 2.02$; round to the nearest simple whole numbers. A ratio that will not round to anything simple usually means a mistake in converting to moles.

check.prompt: After converting to moles you get 0.4 : 0.2 : 0.4. What is the simplest whole-number ratio?
check.solution: Divide each by the smallest, $0.2$, giving **2 : 1 : 2**.

steps.body: Questions give masses, not moles, so the work starts and finishes with a conversion.

check.solution: Oxygen is limiting at $0.1\text{ mol}$, giving $0.2\text{ mol}$ of MgO, so $0.2 \times 40 = $ **8 g**.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. In $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH_3}$, how many moles of hydrogen react with one mole of nitrogen?
2. Write the five steps of a reacting-mass calculation in order.
3. What does "in excess" mean?

**Part B.**

4. What mass of calcium oxide is made from 10 g of calcium carbonate? ($M_r$: 100, 56)
5. For $2\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}$, decide which is limiting given $0.6\text{ mol}$ of hydrogen and $0.2\text{ mol}$ of oxygen.
6. Masses converted to moles give $0.15 : 0.05 : 0.10$. Find the simplest whole-number ratio.

**Part C.**

7. $4.8\text{ g}$ of magnesium reacts with $7.3\text{ g}$ of hydrochloric acid ($M_r = 36.5$) in $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2}$. Which reactant is limiting?
8. For question 7, calculate the mass of hydrogen produced.
9. Explain why a factory making a product from an expensive metal and a cheap acid would use the acid in excess.

For question 5, divide by the big numbers before comparing.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Divide by the big number before deciding what is limiting.** With $0.3\text{ mol}$ of magnesium and $0.1\text{ mol}$ of oxygen it is **oxygen** that runs out, even though there is less of it in raw moles — because magnesium is needed twice over. Comparing raw moles gets this wrong the moment the ratio stops being $1:1$.

**Work the product from the limiting reactant only.** Using the excess reactant gives a number that is too large, and it is the single commonest error in the whole topic.

**Answer what was asked.** Questions ask variously for the mass of product, the mass of excess left, or which reactant is limiting. Each needs a different final line.

**Check mass conservation at the end.** Reactants used should equal products formed. In the worked example, $7.2 - 2.4000000000000004 = 4.8\text{ g}$ of magnesium reacted with $3.2\text{ g}$ of oxygen to give $8\text{ g}$ — and $4.8 + 3.2 = 8$ ✓.

**Keep moles unrounded until the end.** Rounding $0.1333$ to $0.13$ early and then multiplying by a large $M_r$ moves the final answer by more than the mark scheme allows.

**Explain excess in economic terms.** Not merely "to use up the other one" but *the expensive reactant is fully converted, so none of it is wasted* — that is the reasoning a top answer gives.

**When balancing from masses, check the masses add up first.** If reactants and products do not agree, the data has been misread and the ratio will not come out simple.

**Round a ratio only to something simple.** $1.98 : 1 : 2.02$ is $2 : 1 : 2$. A ratio that refuses to round means an arithmetic slip, not an unusual equation.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- *(Higher tier only.)* A balanced equation gives the ratio **in moles**, not in masses.
- $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_2} + \mathrm{H_2}$ means 1 mol Mg to 2 mol HCl.
- **Five steps**: equation → mass ÷ $M_r$ → ratio → × $M_r$ → mass.
- The **limiting reactant** is used up completely and sets the amount of product.
- Find it by dividing each reactant's **moles by its balancing number**; the smallest wins.
- The other reactant is **in excess**, and some is left over.
- Excess left $=$ starting moles $-$ moles that reacted.
- Always calculate the product **from the limiting reactant**.
- Industry uses an excess of the **cheap** reactant so the expensive one is fully used.
- **Balancing from masses**: masses → moles → divide by the smallest → round to simple whole numbers.
- Check that the masses of reactants and products **add up**.
- Keep moles unrounded until the final line.

questions.prompt: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, how many moles of hydrogen react with one mole of nitrogen?
questions.solution: The **3** in front of $\mathrm{H_2}$ gives the number of moles.

questions.prompt: How many moles are there in 10 g of calcium carbonate? (Mr = 100)
What does it mean to say a reactant is "in excess"?
options: There is more of it than the reaction needs, so some is left over
It is completely used up during the reaction
It reacts faster than the other reactant
It is the more expensive of the two reactants
questions.solution: An excess reactant is present in more than the ratio requires, so some remains at the end.

markScheme.description: more than needed, some left over

questions.prompt: What mass, in grams, is 0.25 moles of magnesium oxide? (Mr of MgO = 40)
What mass of calcium oxide, in grams, is produced from 10 g of calcium carbonate? (Mr: CaCO₃ = 100, CaO = 56)
For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, a mixture holds 0.6 mol of hydrogen and 0.2 mol of oxygen. Which is limiting?
options: Oxygen, because 0.2 ÷ 1 is smaller than 0.6 ÷ 2
Hydrogen, because 0.6 ÷ 2 is smaller than 0.2 ÷ 1
Oxygen, because there are fewer moles of it
Hydrogen, because it has the larger balancing number
questions.solution: Hydrogen gives $0.6 \div 2 = 0.3$; oxygen gives $0.2 \div 1 = 0.2$. Oxygen is smaller, so **oxygen is limiting**.

questions.prompt: Moles of 0.15, 0.05 and 0.10 are found. What is the simplest whole-number ratio?
What mass of hydrogen, in grams, is produced when 0.4 moles of magnesium reacts fully with excess acid in Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂? (Mr of H₂ = 2)
questions.solution: The ratio $\mathrm{Mg} : \mathrm{H_2}$ is $1:1$, so $0.4\text{ mol}$ of hydrogen forms: $0.4 \times 2 = $ **0.8 g**.

questions.prompt: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 0.3 mol of magnesium is burned with 0.1 mol of oxygen. How many moles of magnesium oxide form?
questions.solution: Oxygen is limiting ($0.1 \div 1 = 0.1$ against $0.3 \div 2 = 0.15$). The ratio $\mathrm{O_2}:\mathrm{MgO}$ is $1:2$, so $0.1 \times 2 = $ **0.2 mol**.

questions.prompt: Why does industry often use an excess of the cheaper reactant?
questions.solution: An excess of the cheap reactant guarantees that the **expensive** one is completely used up, so none of the costly material is wasted. The leftover cheap reactant is a much smaller loss.

questions.prompt: 7.2 g of magnesium reacts with 7.3 g of hydrochloric acid in Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. How many moles of hydrogen are produced? (Mr: Mg = 24, HCl = 36.5)
questions.solution: Mg: $\dfrac{7.2}{24} = 0.3\text{ mol}$, $\div 1 = 0.3$. HCl: $\dfrac{7.3}{36.5} = 0.2\text{ mol}$, $\div 2 = 0.1$. The acid is **limiting**. The ratio $\mathrm{HCl}:\mathrm{H_2}$ is $2:1$, so $0.2 \div 2 = $ **0.1 mol** of hydrogen.

markScheme.description: divides by balancing numbers and picks HCl

questions.prompt: For question 11, what mass of magnesium, in grams, is left unreacted? (Mr of Mg = 24)
questions.solution: $0.2\text{ mol}$ of HCl reacts with $0.1\text{ mol}$ of Mg. Starting with $0.3\text{ mol}$, that leaves $0.3 - 0.1 = 0.2\text{ mol}$, a mass of $0.2 \times 24 = $ **4.8 g**.

questions.prompt: 2.8 g of iron reacts completely with 1.6 g of sulfur to form 4.4 g of iron sulfide. What is the balancing number of iron in the equation? (Ar: Fe = 56, S = 32)
questions.solution: Fe: $\dfrac{2.8}{56} = 0.05$; S: $\dfrac{1.6}{32} = 0.05$. Dividing by the smallest gives $1:1$, so the equation is $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{S} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeS}$ and the balancing number of iron is **1**.

markScheme.description: divides by the smallest to get 1 : 1

questions.prompt: A student calculates the mass of product from the reactant that is in excess. What effect does this have?
options: The answer is too large, because more product is predicted than can form
The answer is too small, because the excess reactant is partly unused
The answer is unaffected, because mass is conserved either way
The answer is correct only if the ratio is 1 : 1
questions.solution: The excess reactant is not all consumed, so basing the calculation on it predicts **more** product than the limiting reactant can actually supply. The answer is too large.

questions.prompt: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, 28 g of nitrogen reacts with 3 g of hydrogen. What mass of ammonia, in grams, is formed? (Mr: N₂ = 28, H₂ = 2, NH₃ = 17)
questions.solution: $\mathrm{N_2}$: $\dfrac{28}{28} = 1\text{ mol}$, $\div 1 = 1$. $\mathrm{H_2}$: $\dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5\text{ mol}$, $\div 3 = 0.5$. Hydrogen is **limiting**. Ratio $\mathrm{H_2}:\mathrm{NH_3} = 3:2$, so $1.5 \times \frac{2}{3} = 1\text{ mol}$ of ammonia $= 1 \times 17 = $ **17 g**.

questions.prompt: Why is a mole ratio taken from the equation rather than from the masses?
options: Equal numbers of moles have different masses, so only moles give the simple ratio
Masses are always measured with too much uncertainty to use
The balancing numbers refer to grams, not to particles
Mole ratios and mass ratios are the same for every reaction
questions.solution: One mole of magnesium weighs $24\text{ g}$ and one mole of $\mathrm{O_2}$ weighs $32\text{ g}$ — the same **amount**, different masses. The balancing numbers count **particles**, so the simple ratio exists only in moles.

questions.prompt: A reaction A + 2B → C uses 0.5 mol of A and 0.8 mol of B. How many moles of C can form?
questions.solution: A: $0.5 \div 1 = 0.5$; B: $0.8 \div 2 = 0.4$. B is limiting, and the ratio $\mathrm{B}:\mathrm{C}$ is $2:1$, so $0.8 \div 2 = $ **0.4 mol** of C.

questions.prompt:
4.8 g of magnesium is added to 7.3 g of hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

Determine which reactant is limiting, calculate the mass of hydrogen produced, and explain how you would check that your answer is consistent with conservation of mass. (Mr: Mg = 24, HCl = 36.5, H₂ = 2)
questions.solution:
Moles of magnesium $= \dfrac{4.8}{24} = 0.2\text{ mol}$. Moles of hydrochloric acid $= \dfrac{7.3}{36.5} = 0.2\text{ mol}$.

Dividing each by its balancing number: magnesium $0.2 \div 1 = 0.2$, acid $0.2 \div 2 = 0.1$. The smaller is the acid, so **hydrochloric acid is the limiting reactant** — even though the two have the same number of moles, the equation needs twice as much acid as magnesium.

The ratio $\mathrm{HCl} : \mathrm{H_2}$ is $2 : 1$, so $0.2 \div 2 = 0.1\text{ mol}$ of hydrogen forms, a mass of $0.1 \times 2 = \mathbf{0.2\text{ g}}$.

To check against conservation of mass: only $0.1\text{ mol}$ of magnesium reacts ($2.4\text{ g}$), leaving $2.4\text{ g}$ unreacted. The mass that actually reacted is $2.4 + 7.3 = 9.7\text{ g}$, and the products are magnesium chloride ($0.1 \times 95 = 9.5\text{ g}$) plus hydrogen ($0.2\text{ g}$), which is $9.7\text{ g}$ — the two agree, so the calculation is consistent.

markScheme.description: divides each by its balancing number

examTechnique.body:
Read the equation as a **mole ratio**, then run the five steps: equation, mass ÷ $M_r$, ratio, × $M_r$, mass.

To find the **limiting reactant**, divide each reactant's moles by **its own balancing number** and take the smallest — never compare raw masses or raw moles. Calculate the product from the limiting reactant, and if the question asks for the excess left over, subtract what actually reacted from what you started with.
examinerErrors: Comparing raw moles instead of dividing by the balancing numbers.
Calculating the product from the excess reactant.
Giving the starting amount instead of the excess left over.
Treating the balancing numbers as a mass ratio.
Rounding moles before the final step.
Forgetting to convert the mass to grams.
Leaving a ratio as 1.98 : 1 : 2.02 instead of rounding.
Explaining excess only as "to use the other one up".
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer divides each reactant by its balancing number before naming the limiting one, and can say why that step matters — the reactant with fewer moles is not always the one that runs out. It works the product from the limiting reactant alone, subtracts correctly to report the excess left, keeps moles unrounded to the last line, and closes with a conservation check that the reacted masses match the products. Asked about industry, it explains excess in terms of not wasting the expensive reactant.
